title: Roadmap 11: SQL, indexes and transactions
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Joins, GROUP BY versus HAVING, window functions, composite and covering indexes, reading EXPLAIN, isolation anomalies in Postgres, and row locking.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: True or false: `SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE COUNT(*) > 3 GROUP BY dept` correctly returns departments with more than three employees.

options.text: True
options.why: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: WHERE runs before grouping, so use HAVING for COUNT(*).

questions.explanation: Use HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 to filter groups after aggregation. WHERE filters rows before grouping.

options.text: Ann 2, Bo 1, Cy 0
options.why: Right: Cy has no orders, and COUNT(o.id) ignores the NULL.

options.text: Ann 2, Bo 1
options.why: That is what an INNER JOIN would return; LEFT JOIN keeps Cy.

options.text: Ann 2, Bo 1, Cy 1 (the padded row is counted)
options.why: That is COUNT(*), which counts the NULL-extended row for Cy.

options.text: Ann 1, Bo 1, Cy 0
options.why: Ann has two orders, so her count is 2.

questions.explanation: Counting a column from the optional side skips NULLs. COUNT(*) would count the padding row and report Cy as 1.

questions.prompt: Scores are 100, 90, 90, 80. What ranks does `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)` return, in that order?

options.why: Right: ties share a rank and the next rank is skipped.

options.text: 1, 2, 2, 3 (no gap after the tie)
options.why: That is DENSE_RANK(), which leaves no gaps.
That is ROW_NUMBER(), which gives ties arbitrary distinct numbers.
Only identical scores tie; rank still follows the ordering.

questions.explanation: LAG(score) OVER (ORDER BY ...) returns the previous row's value, handy for deltas. Top-N per group: WHERE rn <= 3 over ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) in a CTE or subquery.

questions.prompt: A B-tree index exists on events(user_id, created_at). Select all queries it can serve efficiently with an index seek.

options.text: WHERE user_id = 5
options.why: True: user_id is the leftmost column.

options.text: WHERE user_id = 5 AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
options.why: True: equality on the prefix, then a range on the next column.

options.text: WHERE user_id = 5 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10
options.why: True: the index order gives the sort for free (read backwards).

options.text: WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01' with no user_id condition
options.why: False: without the leftmost column, the index cannot be sought.

options.text: WHERE user_id + 0 = 5
options.why: False: an expression on the column hides it from a plain index.

questions.explanation: Put equality columns first and range or sort columns after. A covering index adds INCLUDE columns so queries can be answered by an index-only scan; a partial index (WHERE status = 'open') keeps it small. GIN indexes serve jsonb containment such as data @> '{"plan":"pro"}'.

questions.prompt: Table orders has an index on status. `EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'done'` shows a Seq Scan, and about 85% of rows have that status. Why?

options.text: Reading most of the table through the index would cost more than a sequential scan.
options.why: Right: low selectivity makes random index lookups worse.

options.text: The index must be corrupt or invalid, because Postgres always uses an available index when one exists.
options.why: The planner picks by estimated cost, not by availability.

options.text: Postgres never uses B-tree indexes on text columns.
options.why: B-trees support text equality and ranges.

options.text: EXPLAIN without ANALYZE disables indexes to estimate the worst case.
options.why: Plain EXPLAIN plans normally; it just does not run the query.

questions.explanation: Read cost estimates and row estimates; compare estimated to actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, since big gaps point at stale statistics (run ANALYZE). The planner also skips indexes for tiny tables, functions on the column, or type mismatches.

questions.prompt: True or false: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement, so on an UPDATE it really changes rows unless you roll back.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: ANALYZE runs the query and reports real timings.

options.text: False
options.why: It does execute; wrap writes in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK to profile them.

questions.explanation: Plain EXPLAIN only shows the planned cost without running it.

questions.prompt: At Postgres's default isolation level, T1 runs `SELECT balance` and gets 100. T2 then updates the balance to 50 and commits. T1 runs the same SELECT again before committing. What does T1 see?

options.text: 50, a non-repeatable read, which READ COMMITTED allows.
options.why: Right: each statement sees data committed before it started.

options.text: 100, because each transaction reads from a single snapshot taken when it started.
options.why: That is REPEATABLE READ; the default takes a snapshot per statement.

options.text: The second SELECT blocks until T2 finishes.
options.why: Plain reads never block on writers in MVCC.

options.text: A serialization failure error aborts T1.
options.why: That happens only at REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE on conflicts.

questions.explanation: Postgres never allows dirty reads (READ UNCOMMITTED behaves as READ COMMITTED). Lost updates from read-modify-write need SELECT FOR UPDATE, an atomic UPDATE, a version column, or REPEATABLE READ with retries.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply about row locking in Postgres.

options.text: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED skips rows other transactions have locked, instead of waiting.
options.why: True: this is how workers claim different queue rows.

options.text: Two transactions updating rows A and B in opposite orders can deadlock, and Postgres aborts one.
options.why: True: it detects the cycle and raises a deadlock error.

options.text: Locking rows in a consistent order in every transaction lowers the deadlock risk.
options.why: True: no cycle can form when order is the same.

options.text: SKIP LOCKED returns rows in strict FIFO order, so no job is ever delayed.
options.why: False: skipped rows are simply handled later.

options.text: Postgres prevents deadlocks by blocking the second transaction's first statement.
options.why: False: it detects deadlocks after they occur.

questions.explanation: Row locks last until the transaction ends. Pessimistic locking (FOR UPDATE) suits high contention; optimistic (version column plus retry) suits rare conflicts and avoids holding locks.
